summary: Defines a mechanism for an access network to give identity selection hints to an EAP peer so it can pick an appropriate Network Access Identifier. It is useful when the peer does not know which network it is joining or has no direct roaming relationship. It is limited in scalability and suited to a small to moderate number of roaming partners. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: When logging in away from home, you may not know which username to use. The network whispers a hint about which one to try.

questions: how do eap devices pick a username
subtitle: Help wireless devices find the right username to use.

tldr.problem: When a device joins an access network, it may not know which Network Access Identifier (username) to use for authentication, especially when the network has multiple roaming partners.
tldr.mechanism: The access network sends identity hint information in the EAP-Request/Identity message, listing available realms (roaming partners) to help the device choose the right NAI.
tldr.outcome: The device can select an appropriate identity and format a decorated NAI to route its authentication request through the correct mediating network. This is limited in scalability and best suited to networks with a small to moderate number of roaming partners.

today: RFC 4284 is an Informational document and is still the specification for identity selection hints in EAP. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: The Identity Selection Problem
sections.content:
The Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) is how wireless devices authenticate to access networks. An EAP peer (the device) may have multiple credentials and usernames to choose from. When the lower layers of the network do not tell the device which network it has joined, or when the access network has roaming relationships with several different mediating networks, the peer may be uncertain which Network Access Identifier (NAI) to include in its authentication response.

RFC 4284 defines a mechanism to help peers make the right choice: the access network can send identity hints in the initial EAP-Request/Identity message, listing the realms (organizations) it can route authentication through. This is especially useful in 3GPP systems interworking with wireless LANs, where a device may have accounts in multiple roaming consortiums.
sections.plainLanguage: When you connect to a wireless network, your device needs to know which username to send. If the network lists the companies it works with, your device can pick the right one.

sections.title: The NAIRealms Attribute
sections.content:
The identity hint information is placed after the displayable string and a NUL character in the EAP-Request/Identity packet. This uses the NAIRealms attribute, which contains a semicolon-separated list of realm names. A sample message might include NAIRealms=example.com;mnc014.mcc310.3gppnetwork.org, listing the available realms.

The proprietary information can appear before or after the NAIRealms list. Implementations can find the list by looking for NAIRealms= immediately after the NUL character, or by searching forward for ,NAIRealms. The realms data ends at the first comma or the end of the string, whichever comes first.

Because EAP does not support fragmentation of Identity messages, the maximum length of the hint information is limited by the link MTU. For an EAP MTU of 1096 octets and assuming 20 octets per hint, a maximum of 50 roaming partners can be advertised.
sections.plainLanguage: The hint is just a list of company names, separated by semicolons. The device reads it and picks which company's system to use for authentication.

sections.title: Deployment Options
sections.content:
RFC 4284 describes three options for delivering identity hints. In Option 1, the access point itself sends the initial EAP-Request/Identity with the hint information. This is the simplest case but requires current access points to support the mechanism and configuring the hints in every access point.

In Option 2, the local RADIUS proxy or server sends the EAP-Request/Identity after receiving an EAP-Start message from the access point. This works with access points that support EAP-Start and avoids the need to configure hints in every AP.

In Option 3, the access point sends an initial EAP-Request/Identity without hints. When the peer responds with an NAI from an unknown realm, the local RADIUS proxy/server sends a second EAP-Request/Identity containing the identity hints. This option requires no changes to existing network access servers (NASes) and may be preferable in many environments.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three ways to send the hints: from the wireless access point itself, from a central server after the device checks in, or from the server after the device tries with the wrong username. The third way works with old equipment.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Risks
sections.content:
Identity hint information is delivered in an EAP-Request/Identity message before the authentication conversation begins, so an attacker can modify it. The NAIRealms attribute must therefore be treated as a hint, not an authoritative indication. Peers should not rely on hints alone to make security-critical decisions.

Unauthenticated hints may cause peers to reveal additional identities, compromising privacy. Since the EAP-Response/Identity is sent in clear text anyway, this vulnerability already exists in EAP. Similarly, an attacker can use a forged hint to trick a peer into choosing an identity bound to a weak EAP method. Requiring strong EAP methods can mitigate this risk.

Revealing the existence of a network that uses weak authentication can help attackers discover vulnerable access points. Therefore, the network being advertised in the hints must consent before hints are sent. Additionally, network operators must be aware that identity hints can affect AAA message routing and may introduce routing loops or other complications in roaming scenarios.
sections.plainLanguage: The hints are not protected by encryption, so an attacker could lie about which companies are available, or trick you into picking a weak security method. This is why devices should not blindly trust the hints.

sections.title: Scope and Limitations
sections.content:
Identity hints are most useful in scenarios where an access network has a small to moderate number of direct roaming partners and the peer cannot determine its network from lower layers. The mechanism is limited in scalability by the EAP MTU: a maximum of about 50 roaming partners can typically be advertised in a single hint message.

Because peers must select a point of attachment before receiving hints, the mechanism does not help a device decide which access point to join when multiple access points are available. In roaming scenarios with many options, the device may need to try multiple points of attachment before finding a compatible one, increasing handoff latency.

This RFC addresses only a part of the broader network discovery and selection problem. Other standards bodies and projects, such as IEEE 802.11, are exploring more comprehensive solutions for helping devices discover and choose networks.
sections.plainLanguage: The hints work best when a network has a few roaming partners, not dozens. And they only help after you pick which wireless tower to use, not which tower to pick in the first place.
